chapter_note.about: Spatial aptitude asks you to picture shapes and moves. chapter_note.simple: Spatial questions are about shapes in space. You imagine folding paper and poking a hole, folding a flat pattern into a box, turning or flipping a shape, or looking at a pile of blocks from the front. The trick is to follow one corner or one point and ignore the rest, and to do the steps in order. Counting also helps: each fold doubles the layers, and a floor of squares can be checked by area and by colouring like a chessboard. For maps, treat the start as the centre of graph paper and add up the steps.

cards.title: Shape properties and symmetry
cards.simple: Fold a paper rectangle exactly in half along its middle and the two halves match perfectly. That fold line is a line of symmetry. A rectangle that is not a square has two such lines, one across and one lengthwise. A square has four, because you can also fold along its diagonals. Some shapes have no fold line but still look the same after a half turn, like a slanted parallelogram. In exam words: a line of symmetry is a mirror line mapping the figure to itself, and rotational symmetry means the figure looks the same after turning less than a full turn.
cards.idea: Fold a rectangle along its midline and the halves match. That line is a **line of symmetry**. A rectangle that is not a square has 2, a square has 4, and a regular hexagon has 6. A shape can also look the same after a turn, which is **rotational symmetry**. These are two different properties, and a shape can have one without the other.
cards.idea_full:
Fold a rectangle along its midline and the halves match. That line is a **line of symmetry**. A rectangle that is not a square has 2, a square has 4, and a regular hexagon has 6. A regular n-sided shape has n lines.

A shape can also look the same after turning by less than a full turn. This is **rotational symmetry**. A parallelogram that is not a rectangle has none of the first kind but has the second (a half turn). A shape is **convex** if the line between any two of its points stays inside it.
cards.definition:
Line of symmetry: a mirror line such that each point and its mirror image are both on the shape.

Rotational symmetry of order k: the shape matches itself after a turn of 360/k degrees.

Regular n-gon: n lines of symmetry and rotational order n.

Convex shape: every segment joining two of its points lies inside it. A shape with a dent (such as an L) is not convex.
cards.intuition_full: A mirror line works like a fold. If a point sits on one side, its twin must sit at the same distance on the other side. For a rectangle, the two midlines work. The diagonals do not, because folding along a diagonal sends the long side onto the short side, which have different lengths. In a square the sides are equal, so the diagonals work too. Rotational symmetry asks a different question: if you turn the paper, does it land on its own outline? A parallelogram does so after 180 degrees, since opposite sides and corners swap, but it has no fold line because folding would send an acute corner onto an obtuse one. Convexity is the 'no dents' test.

example.setup: How many lines of symmetry does a rectangle that is not a square have?
steps: A line of symmetry is a fold that matches the two halves.
Fold along the line joining the midpoints of the two long sides. The halves match.
Fold along the line joining the midpoints of the two short sides. The halves match.
A diagonal fold sends the long side onto the short side, which are unequal, so diagonals fail.

examples.setup: How many lines of symmetry does a rectangle that is not a square have?
steps: A line of symmetry is a fold that matches the two halves.

Fold along the line joining the midpoints of the two short sides. The halves match.
A diagonal fold sends the long side onto the short side, which are unequal, so diagonals fail.
examples.answer: 2 lines of symmetry.

examples.setup: A 2 × 4 grid has cells (row, column) = (0,0) and (1,1) shaded, with columns numbered 0 to 3. How many more cells must be shaded so that the vertical line between columns 1 and 2 is a line of symmetry?
steps: The mirror line sends column c to column 3 - c. So 0 swaps with 3 and 1 swaps with 2.
Shaded (0,0) needs its mirror (0,3).
Shaded (1,1) needs its mirror (1,2).
Neither mirror cell is shaded, so 2 more cells are needed.
examples.answer: 2 more cells.

examples.setup: A parallelogram with unequal sides and no right angle: how many lines of symmetry does it have, and does it have rotational symmetry?
steps: Try the diagonals: folding sends an acute corner onto an obtuse one, so they fail.
Try the midlines: folding sends a slanted side onto a side leaning the other way, so they fail.
So it has 0 lines of symmetry.
A half turn about its centre swaps opposite corners and sides, so it matches itself: rotational symmetry of order 2.
examples.answer: 0 lines of symmetry, and rotational symmetry of order 2.

cards.why: Symmetry and shape properties are the quickest spatial questions. Counting lines is a recall plus a fold test. In GATE: which shape is convex or symmetric, or shading cells to make a figure symmetric.
how: Identify the shape and its type (regular, rectangle, parallelogram).
Test each candidate fold line, using midlines and diagonals.
For grid symmetry, map each column to its mirror and check both cells.
Count only distinct lines.
cards.mistake: Counting the diagonals of a rectangle as lines of symmetry. A diagonal fold sends the long side onto the short side. Only shapes with equal sides (square, rhombus) have diagonal symmetry lines.
edge_cases: A circle has infinitely many lines of symmetry.
An equilateral triangle has 3 lines and rotational order 3.
A shape with 0 lines can still have rotational symmetry.
A concave shape (with a dent) is not convex but can still be symmetric.
connections: Transformations (s5) formalise reflection and rotation.
Tiling (s7) uses symmetry to argue what fits.
Linear algebra (la.matrices_det) represents rotation and reflection as matrices.

cards.title: Folding, cutting, punching
cards.simple: Fold a sheet of paper in half and it has two layers. Fold it in half again and it has four layers. If you poke one hole through the folded paper, the pin goes through every layer, so you get one hole per layer, four holes in all. To see where they land, unfold the last fold first, because that was the last thing you did. Each time you unfold, every hole gets a mirror twin on the other side of the crease. In exam words: after k folds there are 2^k layers, and unfolding in reverse order mirrors every hole across each fold line.
cards.idea: A 4 × 4 sheet is folded twice and punched once. Two folds make 4 layers, so one punch gives **4 holes**. To find them, unfold in **reverse order**, the last fold first. Each unfold mirrors every hole across that fold line.
cards.idea_full:
A 4 × 4 sheet is folded twice and punched once. Two folds make 4 layers, so one punch gives **4 holes**. To find them, unfold in **reverse order**, the last fold first. Each unfold mirrors every hole across that fold line.

A hole that lies exactly on a crease is shared by two layers, so it counts once, not twice. Count k folds as 2^k layers, but check whether any hole is on a crease.
cards.definition:
After k folds (each a halving), a point of the folded sheet has 2^k layers.

A punch away from every crease makes 2^k holes after unfolding.

Unfold rule: undo the last fold first. Each hole at distance d from the crease gets a twin at distance d on the other side of the crease.

A hole on a crease is its own mirror image, so it adds no twin.
cards.intuition_full: Each fold doubles the thickness, so the layer count is a power of two. A punch is one cut through all layers at once, so each layer receives the same hole in its own copy of the position. When you unfold, the paper layers separate and each hole goes back to where its layer lies on the sheet. The mirror picture is the clean way to see where. A fold flips one half of the sheet onto the other, so unfolding flips the holes back, which is a reflection across the crease. The order matters because the last fold lies on top of the earlier ones. Undo the top fold first, then the one beneath. If a hole sits on a crease, the two layers hold the same spot, so the twin and the original coincide and you do not add a new hole.

example.setup: A square sheet of 4 × 4 cells is folded twice (right half over the left, then the bottom half up) and punched once at row 2, column 1 of the folded sheet. How many holes are there after unfolding, and where?
steps: A square sheet of 4 x 4 cells. We will fold it twice, punch one hole, and predict the holes after unfolding.
Two fold lines: a vertical one (right half goes over the left) and a horizontal one (bottom half goes up).
Fold 1: the right half lies on the left half. Only the left half shows, and it is 2 layers thick.
Fold 2: the bottom half goes up. Now only the top-left 2 x 2 block shows, and it is 4 layers thick.
Punch one hole in the visible block, at row 2, column 1. The punch goes through all 4 layers.
Unfold in reverse order, last fold first. Undo fold 2: the hole is mirrored across the horizontal line. Row 2 mirrors to row 3.
Undo fold 1: mirror across the vertical line. Column 1 mirrors to column 4. Every hole gets a partner.
Result: 4 holes. Two folds give 4 layers, so one punch makes 4 holes (if it is not on a fold line). Count k folds as 2^k.
example.answer: 4 holes, at rows 2 and 3 in columns 1 and 4.

examples.setup: An 8 × 8 sheet is folded in half vertically and then in half horizontally, giving a 4-layer 4 × 4 square. One hole is punched on the edge of the folded square that is the first crease, away from the second crease. How many holes after unfolding?

Unfold the second fold: mirror across the horizontal crease. This gives 2 holes, both on the vertical crease line.
Unfold the first fold: each hole is on the crease, so it is its own mirror. No new holes.
examples.answer: 2 holes. A hole on a crease is counted once.

steps: The hole lies on both creases, so it is its own mirror across each.
Unfold the second fold: the hole is on the horizontal crease, so it adds no twin.
Unfold the first fold: the hole is on the vertical crease, so it adds no twin.
All layers have the hole at the same point, the centre of the sheet.
examples.answer: 1 hole, at the centre of the sheet.

how: Count the layers: 2^k for k folds.
Locate the punch relative to the creases.
Unfold the last fold first, mirroring each hole across that crease.
Check holes on creases are counted once.
cards.mistake: Unfolding in the same order as folding, or counting a hole on a crease twice. The last fold is on top, so it is undone first. A crease hole is shared and counts once.
edge_cases: A hole on one crease gives half the usual count.
A hole at the crossing of two creases gives one hole.
A cut shape (not a hole) is mirrored the same way, as a whole shape.
If a fold is along a diagonal, the mirror line is the diagonal.
connections: Transformations (s5) describe the mirror step algebraically.

cards.title: Dice and cube nets
cards.simple: A cube net is a flat pattern of six squares that folds into a box. Picture the row of four squares as a belt wrapped around the box. Squares two places apart in the belt end up on opposite sides, like the front and back walls. The two spare squares fold up and down to become the lid and the base, so they are opposite each other. A real die has opposite faces adding to 7. In exam words: in a straight row of four, squares 1 and 3 are opposite and 2 and 4 are opposite, and the remaining two are opposite.
cards.idea: A net is six squares in a row of four, with one square above square 1 and one below square 4. The row wraps round the cube as four sides. Squares **two apart** in the row are opposite: 1 and 3, 2 and 4. The two extra squares fold up and down to be the top and bottom, so they are opposite each other.
cards.idea_full:
A net is six squares in a row of four, with one square above square 1 and one below square 4. The row wraps round the cube as four sides. Squares **two apart** in the row are opposite: 1 and 3, 2 and 4. The two extra squares fold up and down to be the top and bottom, so they are opposite each other.

On a standard die, opposite faces add to 7: 1 and 6, 2 and 5, 3 and 4. A net is invalid if two squares would land on the same face. A 2 × 2 block of squares can never fold into a cube.
cards.definition:
Cube: 6 faces in 3 opposite pairs.

Row rule: in a straight row of squares, a square and the one two places along are opposite.

Flap rule: two squares attached to the same square, on opposite sides of it, are opposite each other.

Standard die: opposite faces sum to 7. At any corner, 3 faces meet.
cards.intuition_full: Imagine a cube rolling along the row of four squares. As it rolls, it touches the table with a new face each time: the first square, then the next, then the next, then the next. The face under the cube after two rolls is the opposite of the first one, since rolling twice in the same direction brings the original top underneath. That is the 'two apart' rule. A flap off the top edge of the first square folds up to become the top of the cube. A flap off the bottom of the fourth square folds down to become the bottom. They are the two faces not touched by the roll. A 2 x 2 block puts four faces around one corner, but a cube has only three faces at any corner, so it cannot fold.

example.setup: A net has a row of four squares 1, 2, 3, 4, with square 5 above square 1 and square 6 below square 4. Which faces are opposite?
steps: A net: a row of four squares 1, 2, 3, 4, with square 5 above square 1 and square 6 below square 4. Folding it gives a cube. Which faces are opposite?
In a straight row of squares, squares two apart end up on opposite faces. Squares 1 and 3 fold to opposite sides.
The same rule for 2 and 4: two apart in the row, so opposite.

The row of four wraps round the cube as its four sides. Square 5 hangs off the top edge of square 1 and folds up to the top. Square 6 hangs off the bottom edge of square 4 and folds down to the bottom. So 5 and 6 are opposite.
Every face has exactly one opposite: 1 and 3, 2 and 4, 5 and 6.

examples.setup: A net has a row of four squares 1, 2, 3, 4, with square 5 above square 1 and square 6 below square 4. Which faces are opposite?
steps: A net: a row of four squares 1, 2, 3, 4, with square 5 above square 1 and square 6 below square 4. Folding it gives a cube. Which faces are opposite?

Every face has exactly one opposite: 1 and 3, 2 and 4, 5 and 6.
examples.answer: 1 and 3, 2 and 4, 5 and 6.

examples.setup: On a standard die, three faces meeting at a corner show 1, 2 and 3. What is the sum of the three hidden faces?
steps: Opposite faces sum to 7.
The face opposite 1 is 6, opposite 2 is 5 and opposite 3 is 4.
The three hidden faces are 6, 5 and 4.
examples.answer: 15. Check: all six faces sum to 21, and 21 - (1 + 2 + 3) = 15.

examples.setup: Can a net made of a 2 × 2 block of squares with two more squares attached fold into a cube?
steps: Count the faces around one corner of the block: four squares meet at the centre point of a 2 × 2 block.
On a cube, exactly three faces meet at every corner.
When folded, four squares around one corner would have to fit in the space of three, so two of them would overlap.
So the net is invalid.
examples.answer: No. A 2 × 2 block can never fold into a cube.

cards.why: Net questions are short and visual. The roll rule gives the opposite faces without folding in your head. In GATE: which face is opposite, which net is valid, or the sum of visible or hidden die faces.
how: Find the longest straight row of squares.
Squares two apart in that row are opposite.
The remaining two squares are opposite each other.
Check no 2 × 2 block exists and no two squares land on the same face.
cards.mistake: Assuming a 2 × 2 block folds into a cube, or choosing neighbours in the row as opposites. Squares next to each other in the row share an edge on the cube, so they are adjacent. Use the two-apart rule.
edge_cases: A row of four plus two flaps on the same side is a valid net only for some placements.
A row of five squares with a flap does not fold into a cube without overlap if the flap is placed wrongly.
Opposite faces never share an edge.
A die sum of opposite faces is 7 only for a standard die.
connections: Cross-sections (s4) work on the cube once it is folded.
Views of stacks (s6) use the same 3D visualisation.
Counting (ga.quant a8) can count the number of valid nets (11 in all).

cards.title: Cuts and cross-sections of solids
cards.simple: If you slice a loaf of bread straight across, the cut face has the same shape as the loaf's end. Slice a cone straight across, parallel to its flat base, and the cut face is a circle. Slice the cone from the tip straight down through the middle and the cut face is a triangle. The shape of the cut depends on the solid and on how the knife is tilted. For painted cubes cut into small cubes, count by position: corners, edges, faces, inside. In exam words: the cross-section is the intersection of a plane with the solid, and painted-cube counts follow corner, edge, face and interior patterns.
cards.idea: A cone cut by a plane parallel to its base gives a **circle**. The same cone cut through its tip and axis gives a **triangle**. The cross-section depends on the solid and the angle of the plane. For a cube cut into small cubes after painting, count by position: corners, edges, faces and the inside.
cards.idea_full:
A cone cut by a plane parallel to its base gives a **circle**. The same cone cut through its tip and axis gives a **triangle**. The cross-section depends on the solid and the angle of the plane.

A cube cut parallel to a face gives a square. A plane through two opposite edges gives a rectangle. A plane through the three neighbours of a corner gives an equilateral triangle. For a painted cube cut into small cubes, count by position: corners (3 painted faces), edges (2), faces (1) and the inside (0).
cards.definition:
Cross-section: the shape where a plane meets a solid.

Sphere: always a circle. Cube parallel to a face: a square. Cone parallel to the base: a circle. Cone through the axis: an isosceles triangle.

Painted n × n × n cube cut into n^3 unit cubes: 3 faces painted: 8. Exactly 2 faces: 12(n - 2). Exactly 1 face: 6(n - 2)^2. None: (n - 2)^3.
cards.intuition_full: To see a cross-section, imagine the solid made of jelly and the plane as a thin wire. The shape of the cut is the outline of where the wire passes through the jelly. For a cone, a horizontal cut keeps the circular symmetry, so it must be a circle. A vertical cut through the tip keeps the left-right symmetry and shows the two slanting sides, so it is a triangle. For painted cubes, the position decides the count. A corner cube touches three outer faces, an edge cube touches two, a face cube one, and an interior cube none. Corner and edge counts are easy: a cube has 8 corners and 12 edges. Each edge has n - 2 non-corner cubes. Each face has (n - 2)^2 non-edge cubes.

example.setup: A cone is cut by (i) a plane parallel to its base and (ii) a plane through its tip and axis. Name the shapes of the cut faces.
steps: (i) A plane parallel to the base keeps the circular symmetry about the axis, so the cut is a circle.
(ii) A plane through the tip and the axis shows the two slanting sides and the base width.
These make the sides of a triangle, equal in length, so an isosceles triangle.

examples.setup: A cone is cut by (i) a plane parallel to its base and (ii) a plane through its tip and axis. Name the shapes of the cut faces.
steps: (i) A plane parallel to the base keeps the circular symmetry about the axis, so the cut is a circle.
(ii) A plane through the tip and the axis shows the two slanting sides and the base width.
These make the sides of a triangle, equal in length, so an isosceles triangle.
examples.answer: (i) a circle, (ii) an isosceles triangle.

examples.setup: A 5 × 5 × 5 cube is painted on all faces and cut into 125 unit cubes. How many unit cubes have exactly two painted faces?
steps: Cubes with exactly two painted faces lie on an edge but are not corners.
A cube has 12 edges.
Each edge has 5 cubes, of which 2 are corners, so 5 - 2 = 3 are non-corner.
Check the whole: 8 + 36 + 54 + 27 = 125.

examples.setup: A cube of edge a is cut by a plane through two opposite edges. What is the shape of the cross-section, and its area?
steps: The plane contains two opposite edges, each of length a, parallel to each other.
The other two sides of the cut are face diagonals, each of length a√2.
The four sides meet at right angles, so the cut is a rectangle a by a√2.
Area = a × a√2 = a²√2.
examples.answer: A rectangle of area a²√2. It is not a square.

cards.why: Cross-section questions test 3D visualisation with short text descriptions. In GATE: the shape of a cut, and painted-cube counts.
how: Sketch the solid and mark the cutting plane.
Name the cut face by finding which edges or curves the plane crosses.
For cubes cut into pieces, count by position: corner, edge, face, inside.
Check the total equals n^3.
cards.mistake: Reading the cross-section as the solid's face shape. A plane through a cube need not give a square. Check the angle of the plane: it can give a rectangle, a triangle or a hexagon.
edge_cases: A plane through a cube's centre perpendicular to a space diagonal gives a regular hexagon.
A cut through a sphere's centre gives the largest circle.
For n = 2 there are no edge-only or face-only cubes.
The inside count (n - 2)^3 is 0 when n = 2.
connections: Nets (s3) fold into the cube whose sections we study.
Mensuration (ga.quant a10) gives the area of the cut.
Views (s6) project the solid onto a plane, a different slice.

check.q: What is the cross-section of a sphere cut by any plane?
A 3 × 3 × 3 painted cube is cut into 27. How many have exactly one painted face?
How many corner cubes does any painted cube cut into unit cubes have?

cards.title: Transformations
cards.simple: Take one point on a shape and follow only that point as the shape moves. If you turn the picture a quarter turn anticlockwise, a point that was 3 steps right and 1 step up moves to 1 step left and 3 steps up. A mirror in the horizontal axis keeps the left-right position and flips up to down. Do the moves one at a time, in order, because doing them in a different order can end up somewhere else. In exam words: rotation by 90 degrees anticlockwise maps (x, y) to (-y, x), and reflection in the x-axis maps (x, y) to (x, -y).
cards.idea: Take one point v = (3, 1) and follow only that point. A 90 degree anticlockwise turn about the origin sends it to (-1, 3). Another 90 degrees sends it to (-3, -1). A mirror in the x-axis sends the original to (3, -1). Track **one landmark** through each move, in order.
cards.idea_full:
Take one point v = (3, 1) and follow only that point. A 90 degree anticlockwise turn about the origin sends it to (-1, 3). Another 90 degrees sends it to (-3, -1). A mirror in the x-axis sends the original to (3, -1). Track **one landmark** through each move, in order.

The order of moves matters: reflecting and then rotating usually differs from rotating and then reflecting. A mirror reverses clockwise to anticlockwise, and a rotation does not.
cards.definition:
Rotation about the origin: 90 degrees anticlockwise (x, y) → (-y, x). 90 degrees clockwise (x, y) → (y, -x). 180 degrees (x, y) → (-x, -y).

Reflection: in the x-axis (x, y) → (x, -y). In the y-axis (x, y) → (-x, y).

Scaling by k about the origin: (x, y) → (kx, ky); lengths scale by k and areas by k².
cards.intuition_full: A shape is a collection of points, so if you know where one distinctive point goes, and you know whether the move flips the shape, you know the final picture. Rotation keeps the handedness: a shape that went clockwise stays clockwise. Reflection reverses it. Use the point rules to check, since each rule comes from a quick picture. Rotating the point (1, 0) by 90 degrees anticlockwise gives (0, 1), and (0, 1) goes to (-1, 0). The rule (x, y) → (-y, x) captures both. Moves do not commute in general, because a reflection reverses the sense of the later rotation. So always apply the moves in the order stated.

example.setup: Track the point v = (3, 1) through a 90 degree anticlockwise rotation, a 180 degree rotation, a reflection in the x-axis and a reflection in the y-axis (each applied to the starting point).
steps: Pick one landmark, the arrow v = (3, 1), and follow only it. The ghost shows where it started.
Rotate 90 degrees anticlockwise about the origin. v swings to (-1, 3). The rule is (x, y) goes to (-y, x).
Rotate another 90 degrees: 180 in total. Both signs flip, so v lands at (-3, -1).
Now a different move from the start: reflect in the x-axis. The x stays and y changes sign, so v goes to (3, -1).
Reflect in the y-axis instead: y stays and x changes sign, so v goes to (-3, 1). A mirror also reverses clockwise to anticlockwise.

examples.setup: Track the point v = (3, 1) through a 90 degree anticlockwise rotation, a 180 degree rotation, a reflection in the x-axis and a reflection in the y-axis (each applied to the starting point).
steps: Pick one landmark, the arrow v = (3, 1), and follow only it. The ghost shows where it started.
Rotate 90 degrees anticlockwise about the origin. v swings to (-1, 3). The rule is (x, y) goes to (-y, x).
Rotate another 90 degrees: 180 in total. Both signs flip, so v lands at (-3, -1).
Now a different move from the start: reflect in the x-axis. The x stays and y changes sign, so v goes to (3, -1).
Reflect in the y-axis instead: y stays and x changes sign, so v goes to (-3, 1). A mirror also reverses clockwise to anticlockwise.

examples.setup: The point (3, 2) is reflected in the y-axis and then rotated 90 degrees clockwise about the origin. Where does it end up?
steps: Reflect in the y-axis: (x, y) → (-x, y), so (3, 2) → (-3, 2).
Rotate 90 degrees clockwise: (x, y) → (y, -x), so (-3, 2) → (2, 3).
Check: the first move changes the sign of x, and the second swaps and changes one sign.

examples.setup: Now do the same two moves in the opposite order: rotate (3, 2) 90 degrees clockwise, then reflect in the y-axis.
steps: Rotate 90 degrees clockwise: (3, 2) → (2, -3).
Reflect in the y-axis: (2, -3) → (-2, -3).
Compare with the first order, which gave (2, 3).
examples.answer: (-2, -3). The order of the moves changes the answer.

cards.why: Transformation questions come as short coordinate tasks or figure matching. A point-tracking habit beats picturing the whole shape. In GATE: rotate or reflect a point or shape, then match the result.
how: Choose one distinctive point or corner of the figure.
Apply each move in the stated order using the coordinate rules.
Check the handedness: did a mirror reverse it?
Compare the landmark's position with the options.
cards.mistake: Using your own left and right, or applying the moves in the wrong order. Always work in the picture's axes, and apply the moves in the order the question gives.
edge_cases: Two reflections in perpendicular axes equal a 180 degree rotation.
Rotation by 360 degrees returns the point.
Scaling about a point other than the origin shifts the centre.
A mirror image reverses left and right, a rotation does not.
connections: Symmetry (s1) describes shapes that the moves leave unchanged.
Matrices (la.matrices_det) represent rotations and reflections.
Folding (s2) is a reflection across the crease.

check.q: Reflect (4, -1) in the x-axis.
Rotate (2, 0) by 90 degrees anticlockwise.

**Worked example.** Track the point v = (3, 1) through a 90 degree anticlockwise rotation, a 180 degree rotation, a reflection in the x-axis and a reflection in the y-axis (each applied to the starting point).

**Check yourself:** Reflect (4, -1) in the x-axis.

cards.title: Views of stacks
cards.simple: Imagine towers of blocks standing on a grid, and you walk around them. From the front you see the tallest tower in each column, because the shorter ones are hidden behind. From the side you see the tallest tower in each row. From above you only see which squares have towers at all. The total number of blocks is the sum of all the tower heights. In exam words: the front view gives the maximum height in each column, the side view gives the maximum in each row, and the top view shows the occupied cells.
cards.idea: Towers of blocks stand on a grid, each cell with its own height. From the front, you see the **tallest tower in each column**. From the side, the tallest in each row. From above, only which cells are filled. Write the heights as a grid, take the maximum along each direction, and count blocks as the sum.
cards.idea_full:
Towers of blocks stand on a grid, each cell with its own height. From the front, you see the **tallest tower in each column**. From the side, the tallest in each row. From above, only which cells are filled. Write the heights as a grid, take the maximum along each direction, and count blocks as the sum.

Front and side views do not fix the structure uniquely. There is a minimum and a maximum number of blocks consistent with them.
cards.definition:
Height grid: H[r][c] = number of blocks at row r and column c.

Front view (looking along the rows): F[c] = max over r of H[r][c].

Side view: S[r] = max over c of H[r][c].

Top view: the cells with H > 0.

Total blocks = sum of H. With only F and S given, the number of blocks is at most the sum over cells of min(S[r], F[c]), and at least the larger of the sum of F and the sum of S.
cards.intuition_full: A view is a shadow. From the front, a tall tower hides every shorter tower behind it in the same column, so each column contributes only its tallest tower. That is why the front view is a column maximum. The side view is the same idea along rows. A shadow loses information, so many different stacks give the same views. To find the most blocks consistent with the views, fill each cell to the highest level that still respects both its row maximum and its column maximum: min(S, F). To find the fewest, use only as many towers as needed so that every row maximum and column maximum is reached once, which is bounded below by the bigger of the two sums.

example.setup: A 2 × 2 base has block heights (rows are front to back, columns left to right): row 1: 1, 3 and row 2: 2, 1. Find the front view, and the total number of blocks.
steps: Write the grid: [[1, 3], [2, 1]].
Front view takes the tallest tower in each column: column 1 is max(1, 2) = 2, column 2 is max(3, 1) = 3.
Total blocks: 1 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 7.
example.answer: Front view heights 2 and 3, and 7 blocks.

examples.setup: A 2 × 2 base has block heights (rows are front to back, columns left to right): row 1: 1, 3 and row 2: 2, 1. Find the front view, and the total number of blocks.
steps: Write the grid: [[1, 3], [2, 1]].
Front view takes the tallest tower in each column: column 1 is max(1, 2) = 2, column 2 is max(3, 1) = 3.
Total blocks: 1 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 7.
examples.answer: Front view heights 2 and 3, and 7 blocks.

examples.setup: Heights on a 2-row, 3-column base: row 1: 2, 1, 0 and row 2: 1, 3, 1. Find the front view, the side view, and the number of occupied cells in the top view.
steps: Front view (column maxima): max(2, 1) = 2, max(1, 3) = 3, max(0, 1) = 1, so 2, 3, 1.
Side view (row maxima): row 1 is 2, row 2 is 3.
Top view: occupied cells are those with height above 0: (1,1), (1,2), (2,1), (2,2), (2,3), which is 5 cells.
examples.answer: Front 2, 3, 1; side 2, 3; top view has 5 occupied cells.

examples.setup: Front view heights 2, 3, 1 and side view heights 3, 2 on a 2-row, 3-column base. What are the fewest and the most blocks possible?
steps: Maximum: fill each cell with min(row max, column max). Row 1 (max 3): min(3,2) = 2, min(3,3) = 3, min(3,1) = 1. Row 2 (max 2): min(2,2) = 2, min(2,3) = 2, min(2,1) = 1.
Maximum total = 2 + 3 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 11.
Minimum: the column sum is 2 + 3 + 1 = 6 and the row sum is 3 + 2 = 5, so at least 6 blocks are needed.
A stack with 6 works: row 1 has a tower of 3 in column 2, row 2 has a tower of 2 in column 1, and a tower of 1 in column 3 of row 2. This meets every row and column maximum.
examples.answer: Fewest 6, most 11.

cards.why: Views questions test whether you know what a projection hides. In GATE: read a view from a stack, or find the minimum and maximum number of blocks.
how: Write the heights as a grid.
Front view: max of each column. Side view: max of each row.
Top view: mark the non-zero cells.
For the minimum and maximum, use the sums and min(row, column).
cards.mistake: Reading the heights from one side only, or adding the heights in the view instead of taking maxima. A front view of heights 2, 3, 1 does not mean 6 blocks. Only the visible tops are shown.
edge_cases: A zero cell leaves a gap in the top view.
Different stacks can share the same front and side views.
The minimum is at least max(sum of column maxima, sum of row maxima) in a feasible case.
Views of a single column of blocks show the full height.
connections: Cross-sections (s4) are slices instead of shadows.
Nets (s3) and views both need mental 3D rotation.
Matrices (la.matrices_det) hold the height grid, and max over rows or columns is a matrix operation.

check.q: Towers of height 3, 1, 2 stand in a row. How many unit squares show in the front view?
check.a: 6, since there is one column per tower and the squares are 3 + 1 + 2.

check.q: A column of 4 stacked cubes. How tall is its side view?
Heights 2 and 0 in one row of a 1 × 2 base. Top view cells occupied?

cards.title: Tiling and assembly
cards.simple: Before you try to cover a floor with tiles, check the area. If the floor has 25 squares and each tile covers 2, you will always have one square left, so it cannot be done. Even if the area fits, colouring can show a problem. Colour the floor like a chessboard. Each domino covers one black and one white square, so the floor needs equal numbers of both colours. If two squares of the same colour are cut away, the numbers are no longer equal, and tiling is impossible. In exam words: compare areas first, then use a chessboard colouring argument as a necessary condition.
cards.idea: Can a 5 × 5 board be tiled with 2 × 1 dominoes? Each domino covers 2 squares, and 25 is odd, so no. **Check area first.** If the area works, colour the board like a chessboard. Each domino covers one square of each colour, so the colours must balance.
cards.idea_full:
Can a 5 × 5 board be tiled with 2 × 1 dominoes? Each domino covers 2 squares, and 25 is odd, so no. **Check area first.** If the area works, colour the board like a chessboard. Each domino covers one square of each colour, so the two colour counts must be equal.

The colour test is only a necessary condition. If it fails, tiling is impossible. If it passes, you still need to find a tiling or an argument that one exists.
cards.definition:
Area test: (area of region) must be a whole multiple of (area of a tile).

Chessboard colouring: colour cell (r, c) by the parity of r + c. A domino covers one cell of each colour. So a domino-tileable region has equal counts of the two colours.

For other tiles (L-trominoes, 1 × 3 strips), the area must be divisible by 3, and colourings by 3 colours can give further tests.
cards.intuition_full: A tile's shape sets what it covers in every placement, and a smart colouring turns that into an invariant. A domino always covers two neighbouring cells, and neighbours always have opposite colours in a chessboard pattern. So each domino adds one black and one white to what is covered. If the board has more black than white, no tiling can cover all of it. The most famous case is the 8 x 8 board with two opposite corners removed. Both corners have the same colour, so 30 of one colour and 32 of the other remain, and dominoes cannot cover it. Note that passing the test does not prove a tiling exists. Sometimes you must still construct one.

example.setup: Can a 5 × 5 board be tiled with 2 × 1 dominoes?
steps: Area of the board: 5 × 5 = 25 squares.
Each domino covers exactly 2 squares, so any tiling covers an even number.
25 is odd, so the board cannot be fully covered.
example.answer: No. The area is not divisible by 2.

examples.setup: Can a 5 × 5 board be tiled with 2 × 1 dominoes?
steps: Area of the board: 5 × 5 = 25 squares.
Each domino covers exactly 2 squares, so any tiling covers an even number.
25 is odd, so the board cannot be fully covered.
examples.answer: No. The area is not divisible by 2.

examples.setup: A 4 × 4 board has two diagonally opposite corner squares removed. Can the remaining 14 squares be tiled with dominoes?
steps: Area: 16 - 2 = 14, which is even, so the area test passes.
Colour the board like a chessboard. The corners (0,0) and (3,3) both have even r + c, so they are the same colour.
The full board has 8 squares of each colour. Removing two of one colour leaves 6 of one colour and 8 of the other.
Each domino covers one of each colour, so the counts would have to be equal, but they are 6 and 8.
examples.answer: No. The colours are unbalanced.

examples.setup: The same 4 × 4 board has the two corner squares (0,0) and (0,3) removed instead. Does the colour test pass, and can it be tiled?
steps: (0,0) has even r + c and (0,3) has odd r + c, so they are different colours.
The remaining 14 squares have 7 of each colour, so the colour test passes.

A passing test does not prove a tiling exists, so try to build one: rows 1 to 3 form a 3 × 4 block that tiles with 6 dominoes, and row 0 keeps the two middle cells (0,1) and (0,2), which form one more domino.
Total 7 dominoes cover 14 squares.
examples.answer: Yes, it can be tiled, with 7 dominoes. The colour test is only a necessary condition.

cards.why: Tiling questions are short logic checks, and the colouring argument turns a long search into a single count. In GATE: whether a region can be tiled, and how many tiles are needed.
how: Divide the region's area by the tile's area.
If it divides, colour the region like a chessboard.
Count the colours, and compare with what a tile covers.
If both tests pass, try to construct a tiling.
cards.mistake: Treating the area or colour test as proof that a tiling exists. They only show impossibility. A passing test means you must still find a tiling, and ignoring the piece count and area leads to wrong answers.
edge_cases: Area divisible but colouring unbalanced: impossible.
Removing one square from an odd-by-odd board can leave a balanced colouring.
For 1 × 3 tiles the area must be a multiple of 3.
Tiles that can be rotated or reflected may fit where one orientation cannot.
connections: Symmetry (s1) can supply a fitting argument.
Grid puzzles (s9) use the same forced-cell reasoning.
Counting (ga.quant a8) counts the number of tilings.

Area test: (area of region) must be a whole multiple of (area of a tile).

Chessboard colouring: colour cell (r, c) by the parity of r + c. A domino covers one cell of each colour. So a domino-tileable region has equal counts of the two colours.

For other tiles (L-trominoes, 1 × 3 strips), the area must be divisible by 3, and colourings by 3 colours can give further tests.

**Worked example.** Can a 5 × 5 board be tiled with 2 × 1 dominoes?

1. Area of the board: 5 × 5 = 25 squares.
2. Each domino covers exactly 2 squares, so any tiling covers an even number.
3. 25 is odd, so the board cannot be fully covered.

**Answer:** No. The area is not divisible by 2.

**Check yourself:** How many dominoes tile a 4 × 6 board?

*Answer:* 24/2 = 12.
cards.trap: Treating the area or colour test as proof that a tiling exists. They only show impossibility. A passing test means you must still find a tiling, and ignoring the piece count and area leads to wrong answers.
cards.why_full:
Tiling questions are short logic checks, and the colouring argument turns a long search into a single count. In GATE: whether a region can be tiled, and how many tiles are needed.

cards.title: Maps and directions
cards.simple: Imagine you start at the centre of a graph paper, with north up and east to the right. Each time you walk, you move along the grid: north adds to the up number, east adds to the right number. After a few walks you are at some point (x, y), and the straight-line distance back home is the length of the diagonal, found with Pythagoras. The tricky part is left and right turns. They depend on which way you are facing, not on your own hand. In exam words: place the start at (0, 0), update coordinates for each leg, and use the distance formula, keeping left and right relative to the heading.
cards.idea: Start at (0, 0) with north up and east right. Walk 5 km east and 12 km north, and you are at (5, 12). The straight-line distance home is the diagonal: √(5² + 12²) = 13. **Update coordinates** for each leg, then use Pythagoras. Left and right turns depend on the way you are facing.
cards.idea_full:
Start at (0, 0) with north up and east right. Walk 5 km east and 12 km north, and you are at (5, 12). The straight-line distance home is the diagonal: √(5² + 12²) = 13. **Update coordinates** for each leg, then use Pythagoras.

Left and right turns depend on the way you are facing. Facing north, a right turn points east. Facing south, a right turn points west and a left turn points east.
cards.definition:
Coordinates: north is +y, south is -y, east is +x, west is -x.

Each leg adds (dx, dy) to the position.

Distance from the start: d = √(x² + y²). Useful triples: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17.

Turns: facing north, left is west and right is east. Facing east, left is north and right is south. Facing south, left is east and right is west. Facing west, left is south and right is north.
cards.intuition_full: Walking is addition of vectors. Each leg moves you by a fixed step along one axis, so after several legs your position is the sum of those steps, and opposite directions cancel. The net displacement is all that matters for the straight-line distance, which is the hypotenuse of the right triangle formed by the east-west and north-south totals. The only subtlety is turning. A turn is relative to your current heading, so you must track the heading as well as the position. A reliable method is to write the heading after each turn, then convert it to a compass direction before updating the coordinates. Never use your own left and right, since your own orientation as the reader has nothing to do with the walker's.

example.setup: A person walks 5 km east and then 12 km north. How far is she from the start in a straight line?
steps: Start at (0, 0). Walking 5 km east gives (5, 0).
Walking 12 km north gives (5, 12).
The straight-line distance is the hypotenuse: √(5² + 12²) = √(25 + 144) = √169.

examples.setup: A person walks 5 km east and then 12 km north. How far is she from the start in a straight line?
steps: Start at (0, 0). Walking 5 km east gives (5, 0).

The straight-line distance is the hypotenuse: √(5² + 12²) = √(25 + 144) = √169.

examples.setup: A person walks 10 km north, turns right and walks 6 km, then turns right again and walks 2 km. How far is she from the start?
steps: Start at (0, 0), facing north. Walk 10 km: (0, 10).
A right turn from north faces east. Walk 6 km: (6, 10).
A right turn from east faces south. Walk 2 km: (6, 8).
examples.answer: 10 km, in the north-east direction.

examples.setup: A person walks 5 km south, turns left and walks 12 km. How far from the start, and in which direction?
steps: Start at (0, 0). Walk 5 km south: (0, -5), facing south.
Facing south, a left turn points east, not west.
Walk 12 km east: (12, -5).
Distance: √(12² + 5²) = 13, in the south-east direction.
examples.answer: 13 km, to the south-east. Taking left as west would give the wrong direction.

how: Put the start at (0, 0) with north up and east right.
Track the heading before each turn.
Update (x, y) for each leg.
Use Pythagoras for distance and signs for direction.

edge_cases: Moves in opposite directions cancel.
If x and y are both zero, the walker is back at the start.
A 3-4-5 style triple saves calculation.
Direction needs the sign of both x and y, such as south-east for (+, -).

cards.title: Grid constraint puzzles
cards.simple: A grid puzzle gives you clues, like 'row 1 has three shaded cells' and 'column 3 has one'. Start with the clues that leave no choice. If row 1 has three shaded cells in a row of three, all of them are shaded. Then those cells use up part of each column's total, which forces more cells. Before you start, check a simple rule: the total from the row clues must equal the total from the column clues, since they count the same shaded cells. In exam words: write constraints, fill forced cells first, propagate, and use trial and error only at the end.
cards.idea: A 3 × 3 grid has row counts 3, 1, 1 and column counts 2, 2, 1 of shaded cells. The row total (5) equals the column total (5), a good first check. Row 1 has 3 in a row of 3, so it is **fully shaded**. That uses one from each column. Fill forced cells first, then update what each row and column still needs.
cards.idea_full:
A 3 × 3 grid has row counts 3, 1, 1 and column counts 2, 2, 1 of shaded cells. The row total (5) equals the column total (5), a good first check. Row 1 has 3 in a row of 3, so it is **fully shaded**. That uses one from each column. Fill forced cells first, then update what each row and column still needs.

If a puzzle has more than one solution at some point, look for a clue you have not yet used. Trial and error comes last.
cards.definition:
Row clue r_i: number of shaded cells in row i. Column clue c_j: number in column j.

Consistency: Σ r_i = Σ c_j, because both count the shaded cells.

Forced cell: a cell that must be shaded (a row needing all of its remaining cells) or must be empty (a row or column already full).

Neighbour-count puzzles: a cell's number counts shaded neighbours among its 8 surrounding cells.
cards.intuition_full: Each clue is an equation on cells, and forced cells are where an equation has only one solution. Filling a forced cell changes the remaining needs of its row and column, which can force further cells, like a chain reaction. This is why you should always go for the most constrained line first. The sum check is a quick consistency test: both sets of clues count the same cells, so the totals must match, and a mismatch means a misread clue. If you reach a point where two cells could swap, there must be a clue you have not yet used, or the puzzle has more than one solution. In neighbour-count puzzles, you can count a total in two ways, by cells or by shaded cells, and equate them.

example.setup: A 3 × 3 grid has column counts 2, 1, 2 of shaded cells. Rows 1 and 2 have counts 1 and 2. How many shaded cells does row 3 have?
steps: Column total: 2 + 1 + 2 = 5 shaded cells in the grid.
Row 1 and row 2 together have 1 + 2 = 3.
Row 3 has the rest: 5 - 3 = 2.

examples.setup: A 3 × 3 grid has column counts 2, 1, 2 of shaded cells. Rows 1 and 2 have counts 1 and 2. How many shaded cells does row 3 have?
steps: Column total: 2 + 1 + 2 = 5 shaded cells in the grid.

Row 3 has the rest: 5 - 3 = 2.

examples.setup: In a 3 × 3 grid, cells (0,0) and (2,2) are crosses. Every other cell contains the number of crosses among its (up to 8) neighbours. What is the sum of all the numbers?
steps: Count by crosses instead of by cells. Each cross adds 1 to every non-cross neighbour.
The cross at (0,0) has 3 neighbours: (0,1), (1,0), (1,1). None is a cross, so it contributes 3.
The cross at (2,2) has 3 neighbours: (1,1), (1,2), (2,1). None is a cross, so it contributes 3.
Total = 3 + 3 = 6.
Check (1,1): it sees both crosses, so it shows 2. Cells (0,1), (1,0), (1,2), (2,1) show 1 each, and (0,2), (2,0) show 0: 2 + 4 + 0 = 6.

examples.setup: A 3 × 3 grid has row counts 3, 1, 1 and column counts 2, 2, 1, and cell (row 2, column 1) is shaded. Find the grid.
steps: Row 1 has 3 shaded cells in 3 cells, so all of row 1 is shaded.
Row 2 needs 1 shaded cell, and it is (2,1). So the rest of row 2 is empty.
Column 1 needs 2, and has row 1 and row 2, so (3,1) is empty.
Column 2 needs 2 and has row 1 only, so it needs one more, and only row 3 is left: (3,2) is shaded.
Column 3 needs 1 and has row 1. Row 3 needs 1 and has (3,2). All counts hold.
examples.answer: Row 1: all three; row 2: column 1 only; row 3: column 2 only. Without the given cell, there were two solutions.

cards.why: Grid puzzles are logic problems on a small board. Forced cells and the sum check cut the search to a few steps. In GATE: row and column counts, or neighbour-count grids, with an answer that is a sum or a count.
how: Write each clue as an equation on a row or column.
Check the row total equals the column total.
Fill forced cells, then update the remaining needs.
Use trial and error only when no forced cell is left, and test the result against all clues.
cards.mistake: Starting with trial and error, or ignoring the piece count and totals. Always look for forced cells first. A mismatch between row and column totals means a clue was misread.
edge_cases: Row total not equal to column total means no solution.
Two cells that could swap mean an unused clue or multiple solutions.
In neighbour puzzles, edge and corner cells have fewer than 8 neighbours.
A clue of 0 empties its whole row or column.
connections: Arrangements (ga.analytical n3) use the same grid elimination.
Tiling (s7) uses forced placements in the same way.
Constraint satisfaction in AI (ai.logic) generalises this method.

scenes.title: Fold twice, punch once, unfold by mirroring

steps.caption: A square sheet of 4 x 4 cells. We will fold it twice, punch one hole, and predict the holes after unfolding.
Two fold lines: a vertical one (right half goes over the left) and a horizontal one (bottom half goes up).
Fold 1: the right half lies on the left half. Only the left half shows, and it is 2 layers thick.
Fold 2: the bottom half goes up. Now only the top-left 2 x 2 block shows, and it is 4 layers thick.
Punch one hole in the visible block, at row 2, column 1. The punch goes through all 4 layers.
Unfold in reverse order, last fold first. Undo fold 2: the hole is mirrored across the horizontal line. Row 2 mirrors to row 3.
Undo fold 1: mirror across the vertical line. Column 1 mirrors to column 4. Every hole gets a partner.
Result: 4 holes. Two folds give 4 layers, so one punch makes 4 holes (if it is not on a fold line). Count k folds as 2^k.

scenes.title: Cube net: which faces are opposite

steps.caption: A net: a row of four squares 1, 2, 3, 4, with square 5 above square 1 and square 6 below square 4. Folding it gives a cube. Which faces are opposite?
In a straight row of squares, squares two apart end up on opposite faces. Squares 1 and 3 fold to opposite sides.
The same rule for 2 and 4: two apart in the row, so opposite.

The row of four wraps round the cube as its four sides. Square 5 hangs off the top edge of square 1 and folds up to the top. Square 6 hangs off the bottom edge of square 4 and folds down to the bottom. So 5 and 6 are opposite.
Every face has exactly one opposite: 1 and 3, 2 and 4, 5 and 6.

scenes.title: Track one landmark through rotations and reflections

steps.caption: Pick one landmark, the arrow v = (3, 1), and follow only it. The ghost shows where it started.
Rotate 90 degrees anticlockwise about the origin. v swings to (-1, 3). The rule is (x, y) goes to (-y, x).
Rotate another 90 degrees: 180 in total. Both signs flip, so v lands at (-3, -1).
Now a different move from the start: reflect in the x-axis. The x stays and y changes sign, so v goes to (3, -1).
Reflect in the y-axis instead: y stays and x changes sign, so v goes to (-3, 1). A mirror also reverses clockwise to anticlockwise.

Fold along the line joining the midpoints of the two long sides. The halves match.
Fold along the line joining the midpoints of the two short sides. The halves match.
A diagonal fold sends the long side onto the short side, which are unequal, so diagonals fail.  **Answer:** 2 lines of symmetry.

steps.caption: (i) A plane parallel to the base keeps the circular symmetry about the axis, so the cut is a circle.
